title: Political philosophy: Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Mill
note: Social contract theorists ask why government has authority by imagining life without it. Hobbes saw a war of all against all and argued for an absolute sovereign; Locke saw natural rights under natural law and limited government by consent; Rousseau sought freedom through the general will. Mill defended liberty with the harm principle.

read.title: Imagining life without government
text: Why should anyone obey the state? Early modern philosophers answered by imagining a state of nature, life with no common authority, and asking what reasonable people would agree to.

Thomas Hobbes, writing after the English Civil War, held that people in such a condition are roughly equal in their power to harm one another, and that competition and fear would make life a war of everyone against everyone. To escape, they covenant to hand their power to a sovereign whose authority is absolute, because divided authority invites renewed war.

John Locke disagreed. Even in the state of nature people are bound by a law of nature, knowable by reason, forbidding harm to anyone's life, liberty, or property. People form governments by consent to protect these rights more reliably. A government that violates them breaks its trust, and the people may replace it.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued that society had corrupted natural human goodness through property and competition. A legitimate state would let each citizen obey only laws he helps make, as a member of the people expressing the general will.
John Stuart Mill later asked a related question: how far may society, by law or by social pressure, control an individual? Only, he answered, to prevent harm to others.
